lesson.title: Current, LEDs and resistors
lesson.subtitle: Why current needs a loop, and how a resistor saves an LED

video.title: Current, LEDs and resistors
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at his desk holding a dead torch; a pupil beside him. He opens it: one wire hangs loose.
scenes.animation: Torch flickers off; push-in on the loose wire.
scenes.narration: A pupil brought me a torch that won't light. New batteries, a good bulb, and still nothing. Then we looked closer: one wire had come loose. That tiny gap was the whole problem. Today we find out why.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: current, LEDs and resistors, the circuit inside every connected device.

scenes.visual: A battery, wires and a bulb in a loop; dots flow round it. A switch opens and the dots stop.
scenes.animation: Dots circulate; the gap opens and every dot halts at once.
scenes.narration: Electric current is a flow of charge, and it flows only round a closed loop. The battery's voltage, in volts, is the push. The current, in amps or milliamps, is how much flows. Open the loop anywhere, and the flow stops everywhere.

scenes.visual: A pump pushes water round a pipe loop; one stretch narrows and the flow slows.
scenes.animation: Water flows; the narrow section squeezes and the stream thins.
scenes.narration: Think of water in a pipe. The pump is the battery, the pipe is the wire, and the flow of water is the current. A narrow pipe lets less water through: that's resistance. It's not a perfect picture, but it helps.

scenes.visual: Two trays: a coin, a key, a pencil and a cup of salty water; a plastic ruler, a rubber band, a stick and a glass.
scenes.animation: Items drop into each tray in turn.
scenes.narration: Some materials let current through: they're conductors. Metals, pencil graphite and salty water all conduct. Plastic, rubber, dry wood and glass don't: they're insulators. That's why a wire is copper inside plastic.

scenes.visual: A big red LED with a long and a short leg; a plus sign by the long one.
scenes.animation: The LED flips round and goes dark, flips back and lights; then flashes and pops.
scenes.narration: An LED is a light that works only one way round. Its long leg goes to plus. A red LED takes about two volts, and wants about ten to twenty milliamps. Give it much more, and it burns out in a flash.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor at his lab bench holding a 9 V battery and a red LED, far apart. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! I connect a red LED straight to a nine-volt battery, with no resistor. What happens?

scenes.visual: The LED flashes and goes black with a puff of smoke; then a resistor slides into the loop and a new LED glows steadily.
scenes.animation: Pop, smoke; resistor slides in; steady glow.
scenes.narration: It burns out. Nothing limits the current, so far too much flows. The fix is a resistor: it takes the extra voltage and holds the current down.

scenes.visual: V = I × R written large on a chalkboard, each letter labelled.
scenes.animation: Letters write themselves on; labels fade in under each.
scenes.narration: Ohm's law links all three. Voltage equals current times resistance: V equals I times R. Turn it round, and resistance equals voltage divided by current.

scenes.visual: A worked sum on the board beside a battery pack, a resistor and a red LED.
scenes.animation: Each line of the sum writes in as it is said; the LED glows at the end.
scenes.narration: Let's choose a resistor. Two AA batteries give three volts. The red LED takes two, which leaves one volt for the resistor. We want ten milliamps, that's zero point zero one amps. One divided by zero point zero one is one hundred, so a hundred-ohm resistor is just right.

scenes.visual: A wire laid straight across a battery glows red; a hand pulls back. A wall socket with a big cross.
scenes.animation: The wire reddens; the socket gets a cross badge.
scenes.narration: Now one mistake to avoid: a short circuit. A wire straight across the battery has almost no resistance, so a huge current flows. The wire and the battery get hot, and can burn fingers. And in class, batteries only: mains electricity can kill.

scenes.visual: Amina beside a pupil holding a resistor she has just pulled out. Thumbs-up and thumbs-down cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A pupil wants her LED brighter, so she takes the resistor out. Good idea?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a loop, an LED, a resistor, the formula.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Not a good idea: without its resistor, the LED burns out. Use a smaller resistor instead, and keep under twenty milliamps. Remember: a closed loop, the long leg to plus, a resistor every time, and V equals I times R.

scenes.visual: Groups at desks with a battery pack, a bulb and loose wires, touching the free ends to a coin, a pencil and a ruler. The board has two columns.
scenes.animation: The bulb lights for the coin, stays dark for the ruler.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a conductor hunt. Two AA batteries, a torch bulb and three wires are enough. Pupils test a coin, a pencil, a plastic ruler and a key, and sort them on the board. Next time, we'll make switches decide.

checkpoints.prompt: A red LED goes straight onto a 9 V battery, with no resistor. What happens?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — nothing limits the current, so far too much flows and the LED burns out.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with no resistor, nothing limits the current. Far too much flows, and the LED burns out.

checkpoints.prompt: To make an LED brighter, should you take its resistor out?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — without a resistor the current shoots up and the LED burns out. Use a smaller resistor, and stay under 20 mA.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with no resistor, nothing holds the current down, so the LED burns out. A smaller resistor is safer.
